summary: This RFC listed the documents that specified the official protocols of the ARPA Internet, with notes on planned revisions. It was a periodic status report, now only of historical interest. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 901.

eli5.summary: A librarian made a list of the official rulebooks everyone on the network was supposed to follow. Later the list got old and was replaced by a new one.

questions: what were the official arpa internet protocols
what were the official protocols in 1983
which internet protocols are required vs optional
what is the status of tcp and udp in the early internet
subtitle: A 1983 catalog of the Internet protocols in use, with their status and known issues.

tldr.problem: The early Internet had a growing collection of protocols from different sources with unclear standardization status and known problems that needed to be documented.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC listed all official Internet protocols, organized by network, host, and application level, with status designations (required, recommended, elective, experimental), specifications, and comments on known issues.
tldr.outcome: It served as the authoritative catalog of Internet protocols in 1983 and was later replaced by more comprehensive standards documents.

facts.label: Main protocol sources
facts.value: IPTW (March 1982), Internet Mail Protocols (November 1982), Internet Telnet Protocol (June 1983)

today: RFC 901 replaced this document as the official protocols list. RFC 880 is historic and serves only as a historical record of Internet standardization as it stood in 1983.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 880 is a catalog of the official protocols used in the ARPA Internet as of October 1983. It identifies the documents specifying each protocol and notes any revisions, planned changes, problems, or dependencies between protocols.

The RFC explains that the official protocols come from several sources: the Internet Protocol Transition Workbook (IPTW) of March 1982, the Internet Mail Protocols volume from November 1982, the Internet Telnet Protocol and Options booklet from June 1983, and older documents from the ARPANET Protocol Handbook. It is organized as a sketchy outline with each protocol entry describing its status, specification, comments, references, dependencies, and contact information.
sections.eli5: This RFC is like a big list of all the important rulebooks for how the Internet worked in 1983. For each rulebook, it says whether everyone had to follow it or just those who wanted to.

sections.title: Protocol Status Levels
sections.content:
Each protocol receives one of five status designations that indicate how critical it is to implement:

Required protocols must be implemented by all hosts on the network. Recommended protocols should be implemented by all hosts. Elective protocols may be implemented or not, as a system determines. Experimental protocols should not be implemented unless the implementer is participating in the experiment and has coordinated with the protocol developer. None designates things that are not actually protocols.
sections.eli5: Protocols get marked as required (everyone must use this), recommended (everyone should use this), elective (you can use this if you want), or experimental (don't use unless you are testing it).

sections.title: The Network and Host Protocols
sections.content:
At the network level, the Internet Protocol (IP) is marked as required and provides universal addressing. ICMP, the control message protocol that works with IP, is also required. The document notes minor problems with IP's route options documentation and emphasizes that ICMP is an integral part of IP that must be implemented.

Host-level protocols include the User Datagram Protocol (UDP, recommended) for sending independent messages, the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP, recommended) for reliable data streams, and several experimental protocols like EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) and GGP (Gateway Gateway Protocol) for managing network routing. The RFC documents numerous comments and corrections needed for TCP, including clarifications about its push mechanism, listening server behavior, and maximum segment size calculations.
sections.eli5: The basic Internet rules are IP (which sends packets) and ICMP (which helps fix problems). On top of that, UDP lets programs send quick messages, and TCP handles important messages that need to arrive safely.

sections.title: Application Protocols for Mail, Files, and Remote Access
sections.content:
The application level includes protocols for remote login and file transfer. Telnet (recommended) enables remote terminal access and has numerous optional extensions defined in RFC 855. The File Transfer Protocol (FTP, recommended) moves files between hosts with access control, though the RFC notes the need for corrections to its data connection management and clarification of certain commands. The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP, recommended) handles mail transfer between hosts, and the document indicates it has been revised since the earlier IPTW specification.

The RFC also lists several less common protocols: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP, elective) for simple file moving, Remote Telnet Service, Graphics Protocol, and debugging utilities like Echo, Discard, and Character Generator protocols.
sections.eli5: Higher-level tools let you log into remote computers (Telnet), move files around (FTP), or send mail (SMTP). There are also simple test tools that echo back whatever you send or generate random data.

sections.title: Directory and Information Services
sections.content: Several protocols in the catalog handle finding information about the network. The NICNAME protocol (elective) accesses the ARPANET Directory database to find information about users, addresses, phone numbers, and mailboxes. The HOSTNAME protocol queries the registered Internet Hosts database (HOSTS.TXT) to find host addresses and the protocols they implement. The Host Name Server Protocol (experimental) translates host names to Internet addresses, though the RFC notes this specification has significant problems with syntax, protocol details, and extension support, and recommends against further implementation pending revision.
sections.eli5: Different tools help you look up where computers are and find people's email addresses in the network directory.
